deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics by Riemann. It is a French excerpt, with page references, that Riemann copied from V. Regnault, 'Recherches sur les chaleurs spécifiques des fluides élastiques', Comptes rendus 36 (1853), pp. 676–680, séance of 18 April 1853. The excerpt runs as follows.

(i) Regnault's general problem (p. 676–677). Given a quantity of heat Q, what motive work W can in theory be obtained by using it to expand various elastic fluids under practically realisable conditions?

(ii) The old caloric assumption (p. 677). The heat absorbed or released between two states depends only on the initial and final (T, p). In modern terms, heat was treated as an exact differential, a state function.

(iii) Carnot (1824), as developed analytically by Clapeyron. Work is produced by heat passing from a hot source to a cold condenser. Riemann marks with a slash the Clapeyron-attributed remark that heat gained or lost by a gas then depends also on the intermediate states. In modern terms, heat is path-dependent: δQ is not exact.

(iv) The mechanical theory of heat (p. 678). Heat and work are interconvertible, and W is proportional to the heat lost, W = J·(Q_in − Q_out). Riemann first wrote 'différence', struck it, and wrote 'quantité'.

(v) Regnault's numerical estimates for steam engines, using his measured 'total heat' of saturated steam λ(t). In modern notation this is Regnault's empirical formula λ ≈ 606.5 + 0.305 t cal/g; the formula is my identification and is not on the page.
- Non-condensing expansion engine, 5 atm → 1 atm: λ_in ≈ 653 and λ_out ≈ 637, so the useful heat is 16 units. Then 16/653 ≈ 1/40.8, quoted as 1/40.
- Condensing engine with condenser at 55 mm Hg: λ_out ≈ 619, so the useful heat is 34 units. Then 34/653 ≈ 0.052, quoted as 'a little more than 1/20'.
- My check: saturation temperatures are about 152 °C at 5 atm, 100 °C at 1 atm and about 40 °C at 55 mm Hg. With these, λ gives about 652.9, 637.0 and 618.7, matching Regnault's numbers.

(vi) Further notes.
- p. 679: coupled water/ether (or chloroform) vapour engines.
- Ericsson's regenerative air engine: theoretically all heat expended is used for work, versus less than 1/20 in the best steam engine.
- p. 679–680: the list Joule, Thomson, Rankine, Mayer, Clausius, and Regnault's claim to have taught analogous ideas in his lectures.

The page ends at the lead-in to Regnault's experimental 'anomalies' (free expansion, throttling), which continue on the next page. Its purpose is reading notes on the experimental foundations of the mechanical theory of heat, part of Riemann's Naturphilosophie and physics studies.
errors: No errors by Riemann; the copied arithmetic is consistent: 653−637=16 ≈ 653/40, and 653−619=34 > 653/20 ≈ 32.65.

Historically, Regnault's efficiency estimate (comparing the total heat of saturated steam at inlet and outlet) is only a rough proxy for work. In a real adiabatic expansion the steam partly condenses, so the heat converted to work is not simply λ_in − λ_out. A proper Rankine/Clausius treatment gives different figures. This is Regnault's simplification, faithfully copied, not Riemann's slip.
The 1/40 figure is a rounding of 16/653 ≈ 1/40.8 (Regnault's).

results.what: Excerpt of Regnault's statement of the heat-to-work problem and the shift from caloric (state-function heat) to the mechanical theory of heat
results.modern_name: First law of thermodynamics; path dependence of heat (inexact differential δQ)
results.usually_credited_to: Mayer (1842), Joule (1843–50), Clausius (1850), Thomson and Rankine (1850s)

results.what: Steam-engine heat-utilisation estimates 653/637/619 units, giving 1/40 and about 1/20
results.modern_name: Thermal efficiency of steam cycles using Regnault's total heat of steam λ = 606.5 + 0.305 t

results.what: Mention of the Ericsson regenerative air engine as theoretically using all expended heat

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a verbatim reading excerpt of Regnault's 1853 Comptes rendus note, with no original derivation. It only documents Riemann's reading of contemporary thermodynamics, which fits his known physics interests.

checkable.asserts: Useful fraction for the non-condensing engine ≈ 0.0245, i.e. about 1/40.8 (quoted as 1/40)
Regnault total heat at about 152 °C (5 atm saturation) ≈ 652.9 ≈ 653
Total heat at about 40 °C (saturation at about 55 mm Hg) ≈ 618.7 ≈ 619

transcription_corrections: Line 'proportionel à la [-difference-] quantité de chaleur perdue': the image shows 'différence' struck through and replaced by 'quantité'; the transcription is correct in substance.
'système d'Ericson': the manuscript appears to read 'Éricson' (with accent); either way it refers to John Ericsson.
The date '18 avril 1853': the final digit appears overwritten in the manuscript but reads 1853, consistent with C. R. t. 36.
The marginal '(51)' is the folio number, not part of the text.
